writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter II,” how does Austen show family dynamics and anticipation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter II develops the idea of family dynamics and anticipation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter II to complicate the reader's understanding of family dynamics and anticipation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter II within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of family dynamics and anticipation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter II as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of family dynamics and anticipation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Is Mr. Bennet's teasing harmless fun or a sign of a deeper problem? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include fretfully, conjecturing, extracts, adjusting, trimming. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: ““I do not cough for my own amusement,” replied Kitty fretfully.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: Disposed to fret.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Social custom required the father to call on a newcomer before the family could be introduced. Now, why does this chapter matter? Mr. Bennet's playful withholding shows both wit and a certain irresponsibility as a parent. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
